ios.desc:
What is the moon doing tonight? aluni tells you when to look up, and where.

Open the app, or glance at a widget, and you see the one thing that matters: the best minute tonight to step outside and find the moon. Not a table of numbers. A time, a direction, and a picture of the sky over your own horizon.

Only aluni does this:

- Your real hills are on the skyline, so you know when a ridge will hide the moon and when it will clear
- Set a reminder and your Lock Screen draws tonight's moon on its true path above your own horizon
- Point your phone at the sky and the moon finder guides you to it, then tells you to put the phone down and look
- Answer "did you see it?" and share a picture of tonight's moon with friends

The clock behind it all:

- Sun and moon on one 24-hour dial, so you read the whole day at a glance
- Moonrise, moonset, sunrise, and sunset, with the moon's phase and how much of it is lit
- A full month of moon phases in the lunar calendar
- Alerts for the moons you care about, so a full moon never slips past you
- Widgets in many styles and themes for your home screen and Lock Screen
- On iOS 27, a whole home screen page of sky: tonight's best time, the night's times, and a week of phases
- Places anywhere in the world, so you can check the moon over a friend's town

aluni works offline. No ads. No clutter. No account.

Some themes, the weather line, and world location search are part of aluni+, a small yearly or one-time purchase that keeps the app independent.

Terms of Use (EULA): https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/itunes/dev/stdeula/

quotes.text:
Great article that covers some fantastic examples of sun-based time. If you want to read about two more, Seiko has a great article [1] about a traditional Japanese clock (Wadokei) which had moving indices based on the seasons.

The local time we keep today is supremely useful for global synchronization, but is disconnected from the natural world. I came across this example (Wadokei) after making an app for myself to track the moon above and below the horizon and doing some research after creating a similar style clock which uses the sun as the anchor of the clock (high noon is the top of the clock, instead of 12 noon). This one is a full-day clock that shows the hours of the “local time” day as well as the positioning of the sun and moon. The hours shift dramatically during the peak of summer and depths of winter, especially at extreme latitudes [2]. You can really get a sense of the length of the daylight and how it changes by using any of these sun-based clocks.

[1] https://museum.seiko.co.jp/en/knowledge/relation_15/

[2] https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moontime-lunar-clock-widget/id6448401297

Exactly! To each their own for watches and complications. For hunting and fishing there is a (niche?) audience for things called solunar clocks or watches, and recently digital watches/clocks/apps that map the sun and moon in ways physical clocks and watches can't plot yet.
( I'm the developer of one that is a hobby app for viewing the sun/moon inspired by a classic 24 hour clock face https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moontime/id6448401297 )
